Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Martinez: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to jump right into the throughput tuning stuff today, Priya and I will drive, Sean and Leah from Nimbus can stop us anytime with specifics about your traffic shape.
[00:27] Sean Park: yep thanks Alex, quick context, our current p99 latency target is 350ms, burst to 12 rps per instance during morning peak, we saw big tail when we increased sequence length.
[00:45] Priya Singh: okay great, that's useful. quick note, I'm SE so I'll call out knobs we can flip. first, continuous batching behavior — by default our scheduler will try to form batches up to max_batch_size but continuous batching lets us hold a small window to accumulate requests, which helps throughput but adds a small queuing delay.
[01:10] Leah Ortiz: couple questions, how does continuous batching interact with KV cache for chat sessions? like, does it block warm cache hits?
[01:25] Priya Singh: good question, so KV cache is per-session and we do prefix caching. when a request hits a warm KV cache we can short-circuit some compute, and the batching scheduler marks those as fast-paths. However, in transcription there's sometimes a mislabel where the fast-paths get merged into regular batches and that adds jitter — we've seen the transcriber call it "K V cache" or "KV-cache" which is fine but practically you want scheduler to favor assembling homogeneous batches (similar seq lengths and same cache state) to avoid padding overhead.
[02:00] Alex Martinez: adding to that — the main knobs are: max_num_seqs (max sequences per batch), max_tokens_per_batch, batch_timeout_ms (how long to wait to fill batch), and some scheduler flags like prefer_homogeneous and backpressure_threshold.
[02:30] Sean Park: we've been trying max_num_seqs=16, but saw high variance. is reducing to 8 usually better?
[02:40] Priya Singh: yes—empirically for models with mid sized context (1k tokens) dropping to 6-8 reduces padding overhead a lot. for example we ran a config where max_num_seqs=8, max_tokens_per_batch=8192 and saw a 22% throughput increase for throughput-oriented loads while p99 hurt slightly on single-token latencies. tradeoff.
[03:10] Sean Park: okay, and token limits — what's the guidance for token limits per request vs per batch?
[03:20] Priya Singh: keep per-request token_limit aligned to your SLAs, but the batch level max_tokens_per_batch prevents one long request from killing the whole batch. we recommend setting per-request token_limit=1024 for chat flows, and max_tokens_per_batch = max_num_seqs * avg_request_tokens * safety_factor. so for max_num_seqs=8 and avg 128 tokens that's ~8*128*1.5 ~= 1536, but we usually use a higher ceiling like 8192 to allow occasional long tails.
[04:00] Leah Ortiz: that formula helps. what about continuous batching latency SLOs, like how to make sure we don't exceed 350ms p99?
[04:12] Priya Singh: you'd tune batch_timeout_ms aggressively — start at 3ms, then measure queuing delay. also enable prefer_homogeneous to avoid padding. if p99 still high, you can enable fast-path for cached sessions (reduce max_padding_ratio).
[04:40] Alex Martinez: also consider scheduling windows — our scheduler supports token-aware scheduling so if you have many short requests and a few long ones, it can split long requests or send long ones to dedicated lanes (we call them big-token lanes) to keep tail latency predictable.
[05:05] Sean Park: big-token lanes, is that available on private deployments? we are considering VPC on-prem for PHI reasons.
[05:15] Priya Singh: yes, it's part of the runtime — on Redwood Private you can enable lane configs per node pool. caveat: on-prem environment has slightly different kernel selection CPU/GPU perf, so quantify with a short bench.
[05:35] Tom Wu: security question — if we run Private in our VPC, does the batching scheduler still send telemetry to Redwood? we need to keep data in our VPC due to PHI.
[05:48] Alex Martinez: by default telemetry can be disabled and logs can be forwarded to your S3 or local syslog; for Private we support offline auditing and KMS/HSM for key management. we'll send the security deck after this call.
[06:10] Sean Park: great. back to throughput: you mentioned backpressure_threshold — what's the symptom when it's misconfigured?
[06:20] Priya Singh: if backpressure_threshold is too low you'll see request drops or spikes of head-of-line blocking where one slow request stalls subsequent ones; if it's too high you'll accumulate very large batches and suffer padding. we typically set it to about 70-80% of GPU memory utilization for batch allocations.
[06:45] [00:06:45] Speaker 1: um sorry just to interject, when you say GPU memory utilization do you mean model + kv cache + buffers?
[06:55] Priya Singh: yes exactly model weights + kv cache + activation buffers. KV cache can be surprisingly large for long chat histories — that's where eviction policies matter.
[07:10] Sean Park: talk to me about KV cache eviction — we see memory spikes when a few sessions spike to long context lengths.
[07:20] Priya Singh: our eviction policy is LRU by default and we expose a per-tenant cache cap. you can set per-session max_history_tokens to limit KV growth and enable periodic compaction. note the transcriber sometimes writes "compaction" as "compac shun" in the notes.
[07:40] Alex Martinez: one operational trick — warmup traffic. if you can route a small percentage of requests that are likely to hit KV cache (recent sessions) to a warm pool, you get better amortized throughput because those calls are fast-path and help fill homogeneous batches.
[08:05] Sean Park: we've got a warmup job but not granular. are there scheduler knobs to prioritize warm cache hits?
[08:12] Priya Singh: yes, enable prefer_homogeneous and set priority_tag for warm sessions; the scheduler will attempt to group those together. it reduces padding and improves token throughput.
[08:30] Leah Ortiz: quantization — we currently run int8 on a subset, does quant bring down tokens/sec?
[08:40] Priya Singh: quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput per GPU due to better memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency, but it sometimes increases per-token latency slightly on certain op kernels. the tradeoff is usually positive for throughput — e.g., int8 gave us ~1.4x throughput on A100 for a transformer-family model in our tests, but you need to run evals for quality.
[09:05] Alex Martinez: and note there's quant-aware scheduler choices — with quantized kernels you may want smaller max_num_seqs because compute vs memory balance shifts. Priya, show the slide?
[09:18] Priya Singh: sure slide 7 has the knob matrix 
[09:24] [Slide referenced: https://redwood.ai/slides/throughput-tuning#slide7]
[09:30] Sean Park: what's the typical batch_timeout_ms you recommend for chat v synchronous inference?
[09:38] Priya Singh: chat: 3-6ms, sync small requests: 1-2ms. For high throughput, increase batch_timeout_ms to 8-12ms if your latency SLO permits it. but measurements are essential.
[09:55] Sean Park: ok, can we talk about scheduler telemetry? what do we get by default?
[10:02] Alex Martinez: we emit per-batch metrics: batch_size, padding_ratio, wall_queue_ms, backpressure_events, kernel_time_ms; on Private you can route to Prometheus. we also provide per-route token breakdowns in Console.
[10:20] Leah Ortiz: will you share the metric names so our SRE can onboard?
[10:25] Alex Martinez: yes we'll include a metrics mapping in the doc pack.
[10:30] Sean Park: flip to an example config please, cause our team, we run on a 4xA100 pool in Dedicated but for pilot we'll run Private on VMware. what differences should we expect?
[10:44] Priya Singh: main differences: slightly different kernel selection (CUDA driver + distro), network egress latencies, and IO for remote KVS if you use a centralized KV store. For on-prem, enable local KV and set eviction guards. Also set reserve_gpu_memory for OS and sidecar processes.
[11:10] Alex Martinez: and if you're using VPC endpoints make sure the nodepool has outbound to our control plane only on specific ports — Tom we can share the exact list.
[11:22] Tom Wu: yes please.
[11:25] [11:25] Speaker 2: cliff notes — so for Nimbus the immediate steps are run a throughput sweep with max_num_seqs 4/8/12, token_limit 512/1024, and record p50/p95/p99 and padding ratio.
[11:40] Priya Singh: exactly. also capture GPU occupancy and kernel times. one tricky thing: if you see high padding_ratio it's often due to mixed seq lengths — try prefer_homogeneous and per-route batch keys.
[12:00] Sean Park: can you explain per-route batch keys?
[12:05] Priya Singh: per-route batch key is a tag you set on the request so scheduler groups requests with same key; e.g., put route=chat-recent vs route=chat-legacy so you don't mix 256-token requests with 1024-token ones.
[12:20] Leah Ortiz: nice. we have two traffic shapes: 70% short (avg 64 tokens) and 30% medium (avg 350).
[12:30] Priya Singh: then you should run two lane configs — short-lane with max_num_seqs higher (12-16) and medium-lane with 6-8. that'll prevent padding waste.
[12:50] Alex Martinez: let's capture the experiment matrix now — Priya go ahead and propose final test steps.
[12:55] Priya Singh: test matrix: (1) baseline current config; (2) max_num_seqs sweep [4,8,12]; (3) per-route batch keys enabled; (4) continuous batching on/off; (5) quant int8 vs fp16; measure throughput (tokens/sec), padding ratio, GPU occupancy, and p99 latency. run each test for 2 hours under production traffic replay.
[13:30] Sean Park: run length 2h makes sense. what sample size do you need for stable p99?
[13:36] Priya Singh: we'll capture full distribution; 2 hours with peak windows should be stable. also capture 95th and 99th of wall_queue_ms.
[13:50] [13:50] Speaker 1: small aside, does Redwood support automatic fallback to hosted models if our private cluster is overloaded?
[13:58] Alex Martinez: yes, multi-tier routing is available — can fallback to hosted variants with audit logs; but for PHI we usually keep private-only. fallback rules are policy driven.
[14:15] Leah Ortiz: what about model variants and quantization compatibility? if we fall back to hosted we might pick a different quant profile.
[14:25] Priya Singh: scheduler includes model-compatibility checks and will only route to compatible variants. but again audit and data residency need review.
[14:38] Sean Park: quick nit on max_num_seqs naming — someone on infra called it maxNumSeqs in their config and it didn't match our CLI parser, so watch for camelCase vs snake_case in YAML.
[14:52] Alex Martinez: good ops callout. we'll provide example YAML and helm values.
[15:00] [15:00] Speaker 3: let's drill into padding ratio and how it's measured — we saw a metric called padding_ratio but it wasn't clear.
[15:08] Priya Singh: padding_ratio = sum(padded_tokens - real_tokens)/sum(padded_tokens). low is good. we'll add a computed metric: effective_compute_efficiency = 1 - padding_ratio.
[15:25] Sean Park: thanks, that computed metric will help correlate cost.
[15:30] Alex Martinez: another practical trick: pre-tokenization on the client to limit very long tail requests and to enforce token limits before hitting the network. reduces retransmits.
[15:45] Leah Ortiz: about kernel selection — can we force a kernel choice to test? we had variance across driver versions.
[15:53] Priya Singh: on Private you can pin kernel variants via environment flags; on Hosted we auto-select and we can surface recommended driver versions. but pinning is useful for A/B testing.
[16:10] Sean Park: let's talk about monitoring for regressions — is there an alert recipe?
[16:18] Alex Martinez: yes: alert on sudden increase in padding_ratio (>10% delta), GPU occupancy drop, or wall_queue_ms spike; also alert on backpressure_events. we'll include thresholds in the doc pack.
[16:35] Sean Park: fine. last question — how does max_seq_length interplay with kv cache size?
[16:44] Priya Singh: max_seq_length caps worst-case tokens-per-request; KV cache stores per-token KV so if you set max_seq_length to 4096 you need to account for KV size in memory budgeting. you can set per-session max_history_tokens to guard.
[17:05] Alex Martinez: ok we're near the end of the session; quick recap and next steps?
[17:12] Priya Singh: recap: run sweep (4/8/12) with token limits [512,1024], measure tokens/sec, padding_ratio, p99; try lane configs for short/medium routes; run quantization A/B; send scheduler knobs and example YAML; share security doc for Private.
[17:35] Sean Park: sounds good, we'll get the traffic CSV to you and schedule the followup.
[17:40] Tom Wu: also please include the VPC ports list for our security review.
[17:45] Alex Martinez: will do. thanks everyone.
